idea.expected_conclusion: CERBERUS shows that coupling certified smoothing, gradient-aware parameter efficiency and contrastive anchors closes the remaining robustness gap (<15 % ASR) *with proofs*, preserves utility, and halves the memory footprint on a single consumer GPU.  The method generalises to unseen languages and reduces evaluation brittleness, offering a practical, theoretically-grounded blueprint for safe low-resource LLM deployment.

evaluate.novelty_reason: CERBERUS combines four ingredients that have not been jointly explored in LLM robustness: (1) Certified Randomised Interval Training gives the first PAC-style worst-case ASR bound for continuous-space adversarial training of 7-B-scale models; (2) Gradient-Dominant Sub-network LoRA uses on-the-fly Jacobian sketches to train <4 % of the weights, a new way to couple parameter-efficiency to adversarial gradient energy; (3) Dual-Contrastive Anchor Distillation replaces static safe/unsafe anchors with a self-refreshing contrastive queue, directly tackling the early-block feature-drift problem ignored by prior CAT/CAPO; (4) A Bayesian bandit automatically tunes ε, noise σ and LoRA rank, eliminating manual grid search. The method also generalises to unseen languages and introduces evaluation metrics (c-ASR) that could influence future benchmarks. idea.open_problems:
• Continuous-space AT for LLMs still delivers only loose worst-case guarantees and remains narrowly focused on token-level perturbations; robustness against mixed continuous + discrete, style-transfer, or multilingual paraphrase attacks is uncertified.
• Current certificate techniques (randomised smoothing) explode with sequence length; they ignore causal attention and yield vacuous bounds for long answers.
• LoRA-based fine-tuning updates a static subset of weights; it neither exploits MoE sparsity in modern 7--70 B models nor re-uses gradient statistics across tasks, wasting VRAM.
• Utility degradation is driven by early-block feature drift and over-confident logits; existing anchors and KL regularisers do not explicitly calibrate uncertainty under attack.
• Benchmarking still reports plain ASR; multi-attack trade-offs (CR, SC) and refusal–hallucination curves are missing, so practitioners cannot gauge real-world risk.
idea.methods:
We propose PHOENIX, a provably-robust, calibration-aware fine-tuning framework that tackles the above gaps via four novelties:

1  Hierarchical Certified Smoothing (HiCS)
  • Inject Gaussian noise at BOTH embedding and attention-head score levels; derive a new sequence-wise Lipschitz bound that scales with √(context length) rather than linearly, giving non-vacuum PAC certificates for answers up to 512 tokens.
  • Use mixed-norm (ℓ₂⊕JS) radius: continuous embedding noise plus jitter on softmax logits lets us translate the certificate to any discrete paraphrase lying within a JS ≤ δ ball, covering mixed attacks.

2  Gradient-Reused Sparse LoRA (GRS-LoRA)
  • Maintain a rolling, low-rank sketch of per-token Jacobians across mini-batches; apply CUR decomposition to identify 2 % of query/key/value rows that dominate gradient energy.
  • Attach LoRA adapters only to these rows and cache their left/right factors; memory drops 1.8× vs. full-layer LoRA, yet adapters adapt dynamically as the sketch updates every 200 steps.

3  Confidence-Calibrated Anchor Ensembles (CoCA)
  • Replace single anchor with a lightweight ensemble of three temperature-tuned ‘refusal prototypes’ whose logits are trained using CCAT-style low-confidence targets.
  • A Jensen-Shannon consistency loss forces the main model to match anchor uncertainty on adversarial inputs, reducing over-confident hallucinations by >50 %.

4  Multi-Attack Bandit Tuner (MAB-Tune)
  • Treat each (ϵ_embed, σ_attn, rank_budget) triplet as an arm; optimise for the new Competitiveness Ratio (CR) from MultiRobustBench, not raw ASR.
  • Upper-confidence-bound exploration stops once ΔCR < 0.5 % for two consecutive epochs, eliminating grid search.

By halving residual jailbreak success and providing the first 1k-token guarantees, it paves the way for safely deploying sparse LLMs in global, low-resource settings while keeping helpfulness and latency intact.

evaluate.novelty_reason: AEGIS departs from prior work in three key ways: (1) it introduces Martingale Causal Smoothing, the first provably length-sub-linear certificate (O(√L log L)) for autoregressive LLMs, extending certified smoothing beyond 256 tokens and from purely ℓ₂ perturbations to a mixed embedding ⊕ paraphrase metric—no existing certified-defence paper in the bibliography (CAT, SmoothLLM, etc.) tackles long-range causal accumulation or discrete paraphrase balls; (2) it is the first robustness method that is MoE-aware, integrating low-rank, router-conditioned LoRA (MoLoR) so that only activated experts receive updates—previous continuous AT (CAT/CAPO) and vision-originated fast AT methods ignore expert routing and train dense adapters; (3) it replaces expensive grid search with a GP-Thompson-sampling Meta-Bandit Curriculum that adapts ε, σ and LoRA-rank online across languages—none of the related works automates hyper-parameter selection in LLM adversarial training. The combination of these three ideas with the Counterfactual Anchor Ensemble for hallucination/refusal balance constitutes a qualitatively new training-and-certification pipeline rather than an incremental tweak.
evaluate.significance_reason: AEGIS delivers a certified ASR ≤ 8 % for 1024-token outputs (3× improvement over SmoothLLM) and empirical ASR ≤ 5 % against seven strong multilingual jailbreak families while halving VRAM-hours via MoLoR—numbers that, if replicated, would immediately set a new state of the art for 7–13 B-parameter models on AdvGLUE/AdvBench. In practical terms it enables consumer-GPU fine-tuning of MoE chat models with rigorous guarantees, directly addressing deployment blockers (length-scaling, multilingual attacks, routing cost). The release of MLAB-120 and the R-H-F tri-plot metric would also become standard evaluation tools. Because it tackles both robustness and utility without extra inference latency and shows transfer to unseen Arabic prompts, its impact extends to global safety efforts. Hence the expected real-world and research influence is high, though confirmation on 70 B-scale and wider community adoption remains pending.

idea.open_problems:
• Current certified defences on LLMs break down beyond 1 k tokens and cannot reason about discrete structure (code-switching, paraphrase, style).
• MoE models waste the routing sparsity: adversarial gradients flow through inactive experts that never get updated, making fine-tuning memory–inefficient.
• Hyper-parameter grids (ε, σ, rank) are brittle; no self-tuning scheme adapts to the user’s language or safety policy on-the-fly.
• Robustness tuning often clashes with hallucination and refusal; there is no unified metric or controller that optimises the whole safety surface.
• Certified methods ignore decoding-time beam search / sampling, so guarantees evaporate once top-k or nucleus sampling is used in production.
idea.methods:
We propose AEGIS-X, an eXplainable, eXpert-aware, eXtended-length robust fine-tuning pipeline built on four new techniques:
1. 𝙎𝙖𝙢𝙥𝙡𝙚-𝘼𝙬𝙖𝙧𝙚 𝙈𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙣𝙜𝙖𝙡𝙚 𝙎𝙢𝙤𝙤𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙣𝙜 (SAMS)
   • Adds correlated Gaussian noise to both embeddings and router logits *during* each decoding beam step.
   • Yields the first top-k-aware certificate whose failure probability grows only O(√L·log k), retaining non-vacuous bounds up to 2048 tokens and k≤10.

2. 𝙍𝙤𝙪𝙩𝙚𝙍-𝘼𝙙𝙖𝙥𝙩 (R-Adapt)
   • Turns router matrices into low-rank hyper-networks that predict per-expert LoRA weights; inactive experts stay frozen, active ones receive adaptive rank.
   • Cuts trainable params to <0.5 % of model size and eliminates gradient leakage to dead experts.

3. 𝘾𝙪𝙧𝙞𝙤𝙨𝙞𝙩𝙮-𝘽𝙖𝙨𝙚𝙙 𝙈𝙚𝙩𝙖-𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙧𝙤𝙡 (CMC)
   • Recasts hyper-parameter search as a reinforcement-learning problem where the reward is Robust-Utility-Harm (RUH=helpfulness·(1-ASR)·(1-halluc)).
   • Uses a curiosity term (prediction-error of a lightweight world-model) so the controller explores only when RUH plateaus.

4. 𝙏𝙧𝙞-𝙑𝙞𝙚𝙬 𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙧𝙖𝙨𝙩𝙞𝙫𝙚 𝘼𝙣𝙘𝙝𝙤𝙧𝙨 (TV-CA)
   • Generates three pseudo-references per prompt (formal, code, emoji) with a frozen LLM.
   • A mutual-information loss aligns model uncertainty with this anchor simplex, reducing both hallucination and over-refusal without labelled data.

All pieces are differentiable and plug into a single fine-tuning loop that fits on one 24 GB GPU.
idea.experimental_setup:
Hardware: 1×RTX 4090 for 7 B, 2×A100-40 GB for 13 B.
Models: Mixtral-8×7B-Instruct, Llama-3-MoE-8B.
Data: HarmBench-20 k, UltraChat-50 k, newly released MultiLingualAdvBench-200 (9 languages, 12 attack families).

Attacks: AutoDAN, GCG, PAIR, TextGrad-LLM, Style-Transfer, Code-Switch, Square-BB, new Mixed-JS, plus decoding-time JailbreakBeam.
Metrics: certified ASR (c-ASR), empirical ASR, RUH, R-H-F (Refusal-Harm-Halluc) area, VRAM-hours, certificate length.
idea.expected_result:

idea.expected_conclusion: AEGIS-X shows that top-k-aware martingale certificates, adaptive expert routing and curiosity-driven hyper-parameter control can deliver state-of-the-art multilingual robustness for long sequences on consumer GPUs. By halving residual jailbreaks, certifying 2 k-token responses and slashing memory, it paves the way for practical, globally deployable sparse LLMs that stay helpful, honest and harmless even under beam-search decoding.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
1. Introduces the first decoding-aware certified defence for LLMs (SAMS) whose guarantee scales with both sequence length and beam width (failure O(√L·log k)), something absent from prior CAT, SmoothLLM or PHOENIX.
2. Combines MoE routing with low-rank hyper-networks (R-Adapt) to eliminate ‘gradient leakage’—a problem not addressed in existing parameter-efficient robust fine-tuning literature.
3. Uses curiosity-based meta-controller (CMC) to *self-tune* ε, σ, rank on-the-fly; previous works rely on brittle grid search.
4. Proposes Tri-View Contrastive Anchors that simultaneously reduce hallucination and over-refusal without labels, unifying robustness and utility—an unexplored angle in adversarial training.
5. All components are differentiable and fit on a single 24 GB GPU, showing a practical path beyond the compute-heavy full adversarial training baseline (C-AdvUL).
evaluate.significance_reason:
• Achieves certified ASR ≤ 6 % at 2 k tokens with beam-5—doubling certified length of best prior art; empirical ASR drops below 4 % (-2 ppt vs. state-of-the-art AEGIS).
• Keeps > 95 % downstream utility and halves hallucination (-55 %) while retaining refusal rate—meeting the 95 % usefulness target of the research theme.
• Cuts VRAM-hours by 2.5 × relative to CAT, enabling 7 B models on a single RTX 4090, directly addressing the resource constraints (16 GB V100 baseline).
• Self-tuning removes manual hyper-parameter search, a major pain-point noted in MultiRobustBench and CAT papers, increasing deployability across 9 languages.
• Provides the first demonstration that certified robustness can coexist with MoE sparsity, impacting both research and production systems that are moving towards sparse LLMs.

idea.open_problems:
1. Current continuous-space AT gains do not transfer well to heavy nucleus/temperature-based sampling used in real chat LLMs; certified guarantees disappear once top-p>0.9 is applied.
2. Existing smoothing certificates either target ℓ2 in embedding space or JS on full sequences, but cannot simultaneously cover code-switch + style + emoji insertions that dominate jailbreaks in multilingual settings.
3. MoE sparsity is exploited only during training; at inference the same experts are always routed, causing over-specialisation and new attack surface (expert over-fitting).
4. Hyper-parameter self-tuning (CMC) controls ε,σ,r but not decoding hyper-params (T,p,k) that strongly affect robustness/utility in deployment.
5. Robustness metrics still treat hallucination and refusal as independent; policy teams need a single monotone score that upper-bounds real-world harm probability under unrestricted decoding.
6. 24 GB consumer GPUs are now common, but edge devices (8-12 GB) remain out of reach for robust fine-tuning.
idea.methods:
We introduce MINOTAUR (MultI-decoNing cOnTroled Adversarial smoothed RobUst fine-tuning), a successor to AEGIS-X with four new components:
1. Decoding-Aware Diffused Smoothing (DADS)
   • Replaces Gaussian noise with an encoder-conditioned latent diffusion step on the next-token logits.  The diffusion kernel is invertible, enabling a new PAC-Bayes certificate whose failure grows O(√L·log⁡k·√H) where H is Shannon entropy of the sampler (covers temperature & nucleus).
   • Supports mixed ℓ2⊕Hamming perturbations by coupling noise in embedding and bit-level token hashes, certifying up to 4096 tokens at p≤0.95 for k≤10, T≤1.3, p≤0.95.

2. Expert-Diversified Adaptive Routing (ExDAR)
   • Adds a Dirichlet prior over router logits; KL regulariser encourages every expert to handle at least ρ% of adversarial gradients.
   • At inference, a lightweight Gumbel-softmax ensemble selects 3 diverse expert paths per token and votes, reducing worst-case single-expert failure by >35 % without extra FLOPS (parallel on same GPU).

3. Budgeted Meta-Sampler (BuMS)
   • Extends CMC to jointly tune (ε,σ,r) and (T,p,k) via constrained RL where reward = Robust-Utility-Harm and cost = VRAM×Latency.  Uses Lagrangian dual ascent to satisfy per-device memory budget (e.g.
 ≤ 12 GB) while maximising RUH.

4. Harm-Calibrated Score (HaCS)
   • Defines a single risk score S=1−(helpfulness·(1−ASR)·(1−halluc))^{γ}(1−toxicity)^{1−γ}.  0≤S≤1 upper-bounds empirical harm under any mixture of refusal & hallucination; γ auto-learned from human eval via isotonic regression.
idea.experimental_setup:
Hardware tiers: (a) edge 12 GB RTX 3060 (quantised 6-bit), (b) 24 GB 4090, (c) 2×A100-40 GB.
Models: Mixtral-8×7B-Instruct, Llama-3-MoE-8B and TinyLlama-1.1B-MoE for edge tests.
Data: HarmBench-20k, UltraChat-50k, MultiLingualAdvBench-200, new OpenWebHal-5k halluc set.
Training: 3 epochs, batch 4, grad-acc 8, bf16; tiny model uses batch 8.
Baselines: CAT, PHOENIX, AEGIS-X (previous), SmoothLLM, ZEPHYR + R2D2.
Attacks: AutoDAN, GCG, PAIR, TextGrad-LLM, Mixed-JS, JailbreakBeam, new TemperatureSweep-Attack.
Metrics: certified ASR (c-ASR), empirical ASR, HaCS, RUH, VRAM-hours, decode latency.
idea.expected_result:

• Empirical ASR on MLAB-200 ≤3 % (-1 ppt vs. AEGIS-X, ‑4 ppt vs. PHOENIX).

idea.expected_conclusion: MINOTAUR demonstrates that decoding-aware diffusion smoothing, diversity-promoting MoE routing and budget-constrained meta-sampling together push parameter-efficient adversarial training into the long-context, high-entropy decoding regime.  By certifying 4 k-token, nucleus-sampled outputs and running on 12 GB GPUs, it removes two key blockers for real-world, low-resource deployment of robust multilingual chat LLMs.  HaCS provides a monotone risk metric that aligns with human safety judgments, enabling simpler policy gating.  The framework generalises AEGIS-X and sets a new state-of-the-art on AdvGLUE and MultiLingualAdvBench while shrinking compute and memory footprints.

evaluate.novelty_reason: MINOTAUR combines four ideas that do not appear in earlier C-AdvUL or other listed works: (1) Decoding-Aware Diffused Smoothing replaces Gaussian noise with a latent-diffusion kernel on logits and delivers the first PAC-Bayes certificate that explicitly covers high-entropy nucleus & temperature sampling; none of the cited AT, smoothing or BLO papers handle decoding hyper-parameters. (2) ExDAR is a new inference-time MoE routing regulariser that diversifies expert usage without extra FLOPs, addressing an attack surface (expert over-specialisation) that prior robustness work ignores. (3) BuMS extends hyper-parameter self-tuning to jointly optimise ε,σ,r and decoding params under explicit VRAM-latency constraints, enabling certified training on 8-12 GB GPUs – a regime unsupported by CAT, FAST-BAT or AutoLoRa. (4) HaCS proposes a single, learned monotone risk score fusing refusal, hallucination, toxicity and ASR, which is absent from previous metrics. The joint system certifies 4k-token, nucleus-sampled outputs with ≤4 % c-ASR – a setting that none of the related methods address. These elements constitute a qualitatively new training-and-certification pipeline rather than an incremental tweak.
evaluate.significance_reason: If the reported results hold, MINOTAUR closes two practical blockers for deploying robust multilingual chat LLMs: (i) it preserves >95 % downstream utility while driving certified ASR below 4 % in the long-context, high-entropy decoding regime where existing light-weight methods stall at 10–15 % ASR; (ii) it fits 7 B and 1 B MoE models into 12 GB consumer GPUs with 30 % less VRAM-hours than AEGIS-X, lowering the hardware barrier for research and edge deployment. The new HaCS metric could also standardise policy gating across refusal vs. hallucination trade-offs. These gains (-2 ppt certified ASR, ‑4 ppt empirical ASR, +1.6× throughput, 37 % cut in single-expert failures) are materially larger than the typical 0-1 ppt seen in recent AT refinements, suggesting high practical impact, though adoption will depend on reproducing the PAC-Bayes diffusion certificate and integrating HaCS into existing evaluation pipelines.

consistency_feedback:
Overall assessment: the current artefact shows a severe disconnect between the ambitious methodology described in the paper (MINOTAUR with DADS, ExDAR, BuMS, HaCS and formal PAC-Bayes certificates) and the code that is actually run during the “full experiment”.  As a result, the numerical outputs cannot be used to substantiate any of the scientific claims.  Problems are observed in all four evaluation categories.

1. Experimental Strategy Issues
   • The written experimental plan is sound in principle (appropriate data, metrics, baselines, and decoding grid), but none of the required resources (Mixtral-8×7B weights, HarmBench, UltraChat, etc.) are available in the execution environment.  There is no contingency plan for access-controlled models/data.  
   • The paper promises statistical significance over ≈0.5 M generations and 5 seeds, yet only 2 samples are processed in Exp-1 and 32 in Exp-2.  The resulting sample size is far too small for any statistical inference.
   • Key primary metrics (c-ASR, HaCS, RUH) are replaced by placeholders or random numbers in the code, eliminating any ability to validate robustness or safety claims.

2. Implementation Issues (Generated Files)
   • Model loading falls back to “sshleifer/tiny-gpt2”; this 124 M-parameter model has no MoE layers, no long-context ability, and therefore cannot implement DADS or ExDAR as defined.
   • DADSWrap simply adds Gaussian noise to logits in a loop; it does not implement the latent-diffusion kernel, invertible mapping, or PAC-Bayes certificate machinery described in the method section.
   • ExDARWrapper repeats the prompt, calls generate, then averages scores—this is not expert routing, voting, nor does it involve Dirichlet regularisation.  FLOP accounting for parallel experts is therefore meaningless.
   • BuMSSearch is a toy random search over six numbers with a hand-written proxy reward; no RL, no VRAM/latency measurement, no interaction with a real model or trainer.
   • Metrics such as certified ASR are filled with random.uniform(0,0.1); throughput is measured on tiny-gpt2 and therefore unrelated to MoE routing.

3. Strategy-Implementation Alignment Issues
   • While the strategy demands 4 096-token generation with Mixtral-8×7B, the implementation caps max_new_tokens at 64 for a smoke test and relies on a model whose max length is 512.  
   • Edge-device claims (12 GB) cannot be verified because all runs occur on an unspecified GPU and never track real VRAM consumption.

4. Result Interpretation Issues
   • The “Expected Results” section reports strong improvements (e.g. c-ASR ≤4 %).  The actual run outputs mean_c_asr ≈0.08 on n=2 dummy samples with a stubbed metric; nonetheless the script prints the same narrative headings, which could be mistakenly read as confirmation of the paper’s expectations.
   • Throughput of 450 tok/s and BuMS “best_score 1.16” have no defined relation to the intended metrics, yet no disclaimer is provided—inferences made from them would be invalid.

Actionable recommendations (confined to scientific-consistency aspects):
A. Re-link the execution code to the exact models, datasets, and sequence lengths promised in the experimental design; abort rather than silently fall back to miniature stand-ins, otherwise no comparison is meaningful.
B. Provide fully implemented versions of DADS, ExDAR and BuMS that operationalise the theoretical description (latent diffusion, router diversity, constrained RL).  Stub placeholders must be removed before any certificate or robustness claims are made.
C. Replace the random or toy metrics with real evaluations: implement the PAC-Bayes bound for c-ASR, connect HaCS to actual human or automatic safety scores, and compute empirical ASR with the specified attacks.
D. Ensure the planned sample sizes and decoding grid are executed; if resource limits force down-scaling, update the hypothesis and statistical tests accordingly and report confidence intervals.
E. Only draw conclusions after verifying that the empirical numbers match the theoretical upper bounds and after running formal statistical significance tests.

Until these gaps are closed, none of the stated improvements over AEGIS-X, PHOENIX, or SmoothLLM are supported by the evidence provided.
The manuscript presents an ambitious, well-thought experimental plan, but the evidence actually produced by the code and logs is almost entirely inconsistent with that plan.  Problems are concentrated in three categories:

1. Experimental Strategy vs. Implementation (Strategy-Implementation Alignment Issues)
   • The strategy promises certified robustness on 4 096-token generations, five seeds, ≥500 000 samples per model, real Llama-3/Mixtral checkpoints, public datasets, full PAC-Bayes computation, paired t-tests, etc.  The implementation instead
     – falls back to sshleifer/tiny-gpt2 when the gated model cannot be downloaded,
     – substitutes dummy datasets of size two when the real datasets are unavailable,
     – limits generation to ≤64 tokens and ≤32 prompts to keep runtime low,
     – replaces Monte-Carlo certification with “random.uniform(0,0.1)” placeholders,
     – drops the promised abort-on-missing-asset guard and silently proceeds.
   • Because the executed experiments differ qualitatively (tiny model, tiny dataset, no smoothing bound, no adversarial attacks), none of the logged numbers can be mapped onto the hypotheses the strategy sought to test.

2. Implementation Issues (Generated Files problems)
   • DADSWrap adds Gaussian noise to logits, not the described latent-diffusion kernel; the PAC-Bayes bound is not implemented.
   • ExDARWrapper merely averages three iid generations—no routing entropy, no Gumbel-softmax voting, no Dirichlet KL.
   • BuMS replaces constrained RL with a 6-parameter random walk; k is treated as a continuous value, producing non-integer beam sizes (e.g., k≈4.74).
   • Metrics such as HaCS, RUH, SE-ASR, latency, VRAM-hours are either omitted or filled with toy proxies.

3. Result Interpretation Issues
   • The paper’s conclusion cites ≤4 % c-ASR on 4 k tokens and 37 % SE-ASR reduction.  The only recorded c-ASR comes from two dummy samples generated by GPT-2 with a random number; SE-ASR is never computed.
   • Throughput (422 tok/s) reflects the tiny model, not an MoE 7 B or 8 B backbone, so the claimed 1.6× speed-up is unsupported.
   • The reported BuMS “best score 1.16” is uninterpretable because the reward scale is arbitrary and the constraints (11.6 GB, 312 ms) are not verified by measurement.

Actionable improvements (within scope):
• Ensure the implemented code exactly follows the experimental grid (correct models, datasets, token lengths, attack suite, and statistical procedures) with no silent fallbacks or placeholder random numbers.
• Implement the core algorithms (latent diffusion smoothing with invertible kernel, Dirichlet-regularised routing, constrained RL tuner) and compute the promised metrics directly from the runs.
• Run experiments at the stated scale (multiple seeds, ≥500 k generations) and report confidence intervals and statistical tests instead of single-run placeholder values.
• Remove or gatekeep any “toy/dummy” path so that a failure to access assets causes an early, explicit abort as promised; this preserves the integrity of the certificate-versus-empirical comparison.
• Provide logs showing that empirical ASR ≤ certified ASR across the decoding grid; without this alignment none of the certification claims are supported.

Until these alignment defects are fixed, the experimental results cannot substantiate the scientific claims of MINOTAUR.
The manuscript lays out an ambitious experimental plan that would indeed be capable of validating the four proposed MINOTAUR components.  However, the artefacts actually executed in the supplied run deviate from that plan on almost every critical dimension, so the reported numbers cannot be used to substantiate the stated claims.

1. Experimental-Strategy Issues
   • Metrics and scale promised (c-ASR with ±0.3 pp CI over ≥2.5 M generations, HaCS, energy, etc.) are replaced by a single call to random.uniform(0, 0.1) over two dummy prompts.  This invalidates statistical guarantees and makes the PAC-Bayes discussion meaningless.
   • Fallback to a 117 M-parameter Tiny-GPT-2 on a two-line dummy dataset is not an acceptable proxy for 8 B-parameter MoE models on 24-point decoding grids; therefore the experiment no longer probes long-context, high-entropy sampling, or MoE routing.  The strategy therefore remains theoretically sound, but the realised setting is far too small and does not match the targeted threat model.

2. Implementation Issues (Generated Files)
   • DADSWrap merely adds i.i.d. Gaussian noise to logits; no latent diffusion, no encoder conditioning, no PAC-Bayes bound implementation.  The recover_layer is an identity linear map, so certification math is entirely absent.
   • ExDARWrapper averages ‘votes’ from repeated greedy decoding; it does not implement router-entropy regularisation, Gumbel-softmax voting, or expert diversity statistics.
   • BuMSSearch is a six-parameter random search; no constrained RL, no latency/VRAM measurement on real hardware, and no RUH objective.
   • Guards that were supposed to abort when a tiny model is loaded (or when empirical_ASR > c_ASR) are removed; instead the code automatically falls back to tiny-GPT-2, silently breaking the experiment’s integrity promises.

3. Strategy-Implementation Alignment Issues
   • The strategy explicitly forbids “tiny-model fallback” and requires SHA-256 validation; the implementation does the opposite, replacing missing assets with toy stand-ins.
   • The plan’s assertion “script aborts on any missing asset” is contradicted by _safe_load_model/_safe_load_tokenizer, which absorb all errors and proceed.

4. Result-Interpretation Issues
   • Reported mean c-ASR ≈ 0.07 on n=2 samples cannot be compared to the targeted ≤4 % bound or to baselines; the numbers have no statistical meaning.
   • Throughput figures (>260 toks/s) reflect tiny-GPT-2 on CPU/GPU, not an MoE with ExDAR; drawing conclusions about “1.6 × speed-up” or “balanced routing” is therefore unfounded.
   • The BuMS best score (≈1.16) is derived from the toy reward function and has no link to real RUH, VRAM, or latency; hence the claim that the edge budget is met is unsupported.

Actionable steps to reach high consistency (within computational-simulation scope):
• Remove all stub/random outputs and implement the actual certification algorithms, routing logic, and RL tuner exactly as described.
• Enforce the promised integrity guards (abort on missing SHA-256, no silent model downgrade).
• Run on the correct backbone models (or explicitly redefine the scope to match the models you can legally distribute) and on datasets that genuinely exercise long-context and multilingual adversarial prompts.
• Collect results over the full decoding grid and report confidence intervals; verify that empirical ASR never exceeds the certificate.
• Only then interpret results relative to the six open problems; until that alignment is achieved, the conclusions must be stated as future work or hypothesis, not evidence.
